Tax

Help your clients make sure new employees are paid correctly from day one

Getting new starter details right first time helps your clients avoid extra administration, reduces payroll errors and reassures employees that they are being paid correctly from day one.

Your clients can help make the process smoother by following 3 simple steps:

Ask new employees for key personal information before they start, including their full name, date of birth and National Insurance number.

Use a P45 or the online starter checklist to set up PAYE correctly and send accurate information to HMRC.

Encourage new employees to download the HMRC app. They can use it to check their tax code, National Insurance number, annual tax summary and employment history.

Share these steps with your clients to help them avoid common new starter errors.

Guidelines for Compliance — GfC22 — help to prevent payroll errors and PAYE RTI disputed charges

HMRC has recently published new Guidelines for Compliance: Help to prevent payroll errors and PAYE RTI disputed charges.

These guidelines are for employers and those who process payroll on behalf of employers. They may also be useful for tax agents and professional bodies advising clients or members about their payroll obligations.

A Real Time Information (RTI) disputed charge occurs when the amount an employer believes they owe in PAYE differs from the amount shown on HMRC’s systems. This can result in either a credit or debit on the employers account.

The guidelines provide practical support to help employers avoid payroll submission errors, reducing the likelihood of disputed charges arising.

The guidelines help by:

providing background information on RTI disputed charges

highlighting the most common errors

explaining how to avoid these errors

explaining what to do if a mistake is made

Read more information on the Guidelines for Compliance collection.

Guidelines for Compliance — GfC21 — help with VAT on cryptoassets

HMRC published new Guidelines for Compliance to help with VAT on cryptoassets on 15 October 2026.

The guidelines are for UK and overseas businesses involved in cryptoasset transactions where UK VAT may apply. This includes:

businesses that sell or exchange cryptoassets

artists and creators who supply cryptoassets directly to customers

operators of digital platforms or marketplaces through which other people make supplies

The guidelines may also be useful to agents and advisers acting for these businesses.

They bring together existing VAT principles and explain how they apply to cryptoasset activities. They do not introduce new VAT rules.

The guidelines explain:

what HMRC means by cryptoassets for the purposes of the guidelines

when a business may need to register for VAT

how the VAT treatment depends on what is supplied and how it is used, rather than the name or description of a token

what customer and transaction information businesses should collect and retain

how to establish whether a customer is a business or private consumer and where the customer belongs

how the place of supply and electronically supplied services rules may apply

when a digital platform or marketplace may be responsible for accounting for VAT

what to do if a business identifies a previous VAT error or is unsure about the correct treatment

Agents should consider the guidelines when advising clients that sell or exchange cryptoassets or facilitate supplies of them.

Agents should help clients check that they have:

correctly identified the underlying supply

met any VAT registration obligations

collected enough evidence of the customer’s status and location

established who is responsible for accounting for VAT when a platform is involved

Following the guidelines will help businesses reduce the risk of errors, VAT adjustments and penalties.

Changes to Climate Change Levy

HMRC is modernising the administration of the Climate Change Levy (CCL). As part of these changes, existing customers will receive a new CCL reference number.

The updated service is planned to go live early 2027. HMRC will contact affected customers before they need to take any action and will tell them when to start using their new reference number.

Until then you and your clients should continue to meet existing CCL obligations and follow current CCL guidance.

What you need to do now

If you have clients who file Climate Change Levy returns, you should:

make sure relevant colleagues and clients are aware that changes are planned from early 2027

continue to follow current CCL guidance until HMRC publishes updated instructions

look out for further information from HMRC about new reference numbers, access to the updated service, enrolment and Direct Debit arrangements in early 2027

make sure HMRC holds the correct business contact details

New Climate Change Levy reference numbers

HMRC will tell existing customers about their new CCL reference number before they need to use it. We will also explain when and where to use the new reference.

Direct Debit arrangements

HMRC will write to affected customers about any action they need to take in relation to their Direct Debit. The letter will explain what to do and when.

Customers should not cancel or change an existing Direct Debit unless HMRC tells them to.

Check contact details

Make sure HMRC holds the correct contact details for your clients.

You or your clients can contact the Climate Change Levy helpline if contact details need to be updated.

Further information

Continue to follow the current Climate Change Levy guidance until HMRC publishes further information about the changes.

Corporate Interest Restriction: reporting companies

Background

Corporate Interest Restriction (CIR) allows groups to appoint a reporting company which facilitates the administration of the rules, including filing of interest restriction returns (IRRs) for the group.

HMRC introduced changes to the CIR rules in Finance Act 2026. These changes follow the announcement about the application of the administration rules in issue 130 of Agent Update. The changes aim to make it simpler for customers to comply with the rules.

A reminder for periods ending on or before 30 March 2026

For periods ending before 31 March 2026, the existing rules broadly continue to apply. Where a reporting company appointment has not already been made, groups must still notify HMRC of these appointments. Use the existing approved filing methods such as the online form on GOV.UK or commercial software. This will be particularly relevant, for example, for groups that are in the process of preparing their IRR for the year ended 31 December 2025.

Periods ending on or after 31 March 2026

For periods of account ending on or after 31 March 2026, groups no longer need to make reporting company appointments ‘by notice’ to HMRC. Instead, they will in future be required to disclose details of these appointments in their IRR for that period. Reporting appointments only have effect for the specific period of account.

HMRC is in the process of updating the IT software to enable this disclosure. The legal obligation to disclose this additional information will be put in place when the IT changes are nearer completion. For the time being, continue to file using the existing forms or software. We will provide further updates.

If you have any queries or concerns regarding the reporting requirements, contact the CIR team by email cirworkinggroup@hmrc.gov.uk.

Publication of new guidance on anti-avoidance powers

We have recently published 2 new pages of guidance on GOV.UK on anti-avoidance powers.

Prohibition of the promotion of certain tax avoidance arrangements

Read the prohibition of the promotion of certain tax avoidance arrangements.

This guidance describes the legislation in sections 159 to 165 of the Finance Act 2026. The legislation introduced new rules prohibiting the promotion of certain tax avoidance arrangements.

The legislation makes it an offence to promote arrangements where:

the arrangements have been or are likely to be marketed as providing a particular tax advantage but there is no realistic prospect that the advantage will be achieved

the arrangements fall within a type specified in regulations made by HMRC.

The guidance explains:

which arrangements are prohibited

what is meant by the term ‘promotion’

the civil and criminal sanctions that apply when the legislation is breached, including who may be held liable for those sanctions

It is important that you review the guidance to make sure that you and your clients comply with the legislation. The legislation applies whether or not you are aware of it and does not require prior notice.

Legal professional privilege

Read HMRC’s view on how legal professional privilege interacts with anti-avoidance powers.

Legal professional privilege is a vital principle and fundamental right.

The guidance explains how legal professional privilege applies when HMRC deals with tax avoidance cases, including:

disputes

disclosure requirements

enabler penalties

declarations

the publication of information

Business Income Manual updates

HMRC published updates to the Business Income Manual on 1 July 2026. These changes relate to interest deductions and withdrawal of capital from businesses. Updates were made to pages BIM45675 to BIM45730.

Why we made the changes

We made these changes to improve the clarity and consistency of the guidance on:

the deductibility of interest

how the wholly and exclusively test applies

The changes take account of feedback from stakeholders and our operational experience.

These are not changes to the law, and they do not introduce a new interpretation of it.

The legal test has not changed

The statutory test remains section 34 of the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005.

Whether interest is deductible depends on whether the borrowing was incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade or property business. This is judged by reference to all the relevant facts and circumstances.

Deductibility cannot be determined solely by asking whether borrowing replaces capital previously introduced into a business. Nor can it be determined solely by reference to the balance on a proprietor’s capital account. Those factors may be relevant, but they are not decisive on their own.

The central question is the purpose of the borrowing. The purpose of the borrowing and the use of the borrowed funds must show whether the borrowing was for the business or for a private purpose.

Why we removed the numerical examples

We removed the numerical examples and capital account calculations from the guidance. This does not mean this information is irrelevant.

The aim of the revision was to place greater emphasis on the underlying legal principles. Looking at accounting mechanics in isolation can obscure the fundamental question of purpose, which is what actually determines the outcome.

What the new examples illustrate

The revised examples illustrate how these principles apply to factual situations that often arise in practice. The outcome in any particular case will depend on a careful evaluation of the evidence relating to the borrowing concerned.

This reflects HMRC’s long-standing approach to the ‘wholly and exclusively’ test, which depends on the facts of each case.

Examples illustrate particular factual scenarios. They should be read alongside the wider guidance, relevant legislation and case law. No single example can provide a complete statement of HMRC’s interpretation of the law for every circumstance.

Keeping the guidance under review

HMRC will continue to review the guidance to make sure it remains accurate, clear and consistent. As part of this process, we will consider feedback from:

taxpayers

agents

representative bodies

Stamp Duty Land Tax Group Relief

As announced at Budget 2026, the government has amended the Stamp Duty Land Tax group relief rules. The changes mean that a winding up of a vendor does not prevent the relief from being clawed back within the usual 3 year period if the purchasing company later leaves the group. The changes apply to transactions with an effective date on or after 29 October 2026.

Read more about Stamp Duty Land Tax — changes to group relief.

New guidance for reporting under the Cryptoasset Reporting Framework

New information is available to help reporting Cryptoasset Service Providers prepare for reporting under the Cryptoasset Reporting Framework (CARF). This includes requirements for reporting files and details of the checks HMRC will apply when reports are submitted.

If you are working on behalf of a Reporting Cryptoasset Service Provider, you will need to upload your report to HMRC’s online service before 31 May 2027. The service is not yet available. We will update the guidance when it is available.

Subscribe to our CARF guidance pages to be notified when:

further guidance is published

more information about the reporting service is available

the submission window is confirmed

Capital Gains Tax measures announced at Budget 2026

The government announced a number of measures affecting Capital Gains Tax at the Budget on 28 October 2026.

There is a list of measures that took effect from 28 October 2026.

Capital sums received for surrendering rights

This measure clarifies that, for Capital Gains purposes, a capital sum for surrender of rights includes a capital sum received under a contract for loss of right under that contract.

Preventing protected cell company avoidance

This measure changes the rules that apply to gains made by non-resident close companies that are attributed to UK resident individuals, trusts and companies that hold assets through a non-UK resident protected cell company.

Temporarily migrated trusts

This measure means that Capital Gains Tax exit charges will not apply to temporarily migrated trusts if they become UK resident because one of their trustees moves to the UK and they cease to be UK resident by the end of the following tax year.

UK property returns

Late filing penalties will stop once the disposal is subsequently reported through Self Assessment.

There are further Capital Gains Tax changes which will take effect from 6 April 2027.

Business Asset Disposal Relief

The lifetime limit will reduce from £1 million to £500,000 for qualifying disposals.

Capital Gains Tax relief for gifts of business assets

This measure includes as ‘chargeable assets’ those assets that would be chargeable but for being within the substantial shareholding exemption or the intangible fixed assets regime such as goodwill created or acquired on or after 1 April 2002.

Introduction of a new Capital Gains Tax Founder’s Relief

This measure introduces a new Capital Gains Tax relief for eligible founders and early investors who dispose of qualifying shares or securities in high-growth, innovative companies that meet all the relevant criteria. It will apply to qualifying disposals from 6 April 2027.

Further information about these measures will be provided in future updates.

New guidance on the International Controlled Transactions Schedule

Regulations for the International Controlled Transactions Schedule (ICTS) were laid before the House of Commons on 4 November 2026.

HMRC has published guidance on the regulations in the International Manual at INTM917300 and INTM917400.

HMRC aims to publish the ICTS notice on 26 November 2026 and detailed guidance on the ICTS notice by 31 December 2026.

The ICTS is a new annual reporting requirement for businesses within scope of UK transfer pricing or permanent establishment rules.

Businesses within scope will need to provide HMRC with specified information about cross-border related party transactions for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

Agents and advisers should use the guidance to help identify clients who may be affected and help them understand the requirements.

Share the guidance with relevant networks and clients.

Important changes to Automatic Exchange of Information — action required

This article covers 2 key deadlines you need to be aware of:

the Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI) will temporarily close from 15 December 2026 until early January 2027

Electronic Money Institutions must register for the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) by 31 January 2027

These changes may affect financial institutions you represent.

AEOI service closing on 15 December 2026 — what you need to do

HMRC is introducing a new digital service for Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) reporting.

To prepare for this, the current AEOI service will close at 3pm on 15 December 2026. The first phase of the new service opens in early January 2027.

While the service is unavailable, you and your clients will not be able to:

register

submit CRS or FATCA reports

correct or amend CRS or FATCA reports

You must complete any outstanding CRS and FATCA submissions, corrections and amendments before 3pm on 15 December 2026.

You should also:

check that your contact details are up to date

tell relevant colleagues and clients that the service is closing

We will provide an update when the first phase of the new service is live. Existing AEOI service users will not need to register again.

If you have clients who are Electronic Money Institutions

As previously shared in Agent Updates, changes to CRS 2.0 implemented from 1 January 2026 mean that Electronic Money Institutions have new obligations.

Read more in previous Agent Update editions:

December Agent Update

May Agent Update

If your clients hold Specified Electronic Money Products or Central Bank Digital Currencies on behalf of customers, they are considered a Depository Institution for CRS purposes.

Clients who are within scope will have registration, due diligence, and reporting obligations to HMRC. They must register for CRS by 31 January 2027, even if they do not have any reportable accounts.

Clients who have already registered do not need to do it again.

Help test the registration service

We are looking for Electronic Money Institution volunteers to test the new CRS registration service before it opens to everyone. Volunteers will receive dedicated support with registration. Their feedback will help us improve the service for other users.

To take part, Electronic Money Institutions should email nimco.huseen@digital.hmrc.gov.uk with ‘CRS Beta Testing’ in the subject line.

Share this information with relevant clients.

Key dates

15 December 2026 at 3pm: the current service closes

early January 2027: the first phase of the new service opens

31 January 2027: deadline for Electronic Money Institutions to register for CRS

Reporting functionality will be introduced later in 2027. We will publish guidance in advance to explain what reporting financial institutions need to do.

Where to find help

Read more on the Automatic Exchange of Information agreements collection page for guidance on CRS registration and reporting.

For technical guidance on CRS, including due diligence requirements and an overview of the new penalty regime, read the International Exchange of Information Manual.

If you still have questions, email aeoi.enquiries@hmrc.gov.uk.

Updated guidance on mandatory reporting of benefits in kind

We are updating our guidance to prepare for mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind. This will help agents, stakeholders, employers and third-party benefit providers get ready for the changes with detailed information and examples to help them prepare well ahead of mandatory reporting of benefits in kind in real time from 6 April 2027.

From 6 April 2027, company cars, car fuel, vans, van fuel, and medical benefits will no longer be included in the employees’ tax codes.

Employers will need to:

report these benefits through payroll

deduct tax due directly from employees pay in real time

pay the associated Class 1A National Insurance contributions

Globally mobile employees

Agents are encouraged to inform their clients that employers will have the option to exclude eligible globally mobile employees from mandatory payrolling through a new exception cases service.

Employers must complete the new online exception cases form available from 5 November 2026 to notify HMRC.

Employers should continue to use existing year-end reporting arrangements for these employees through forms P11D and P11D(b). Our updated guidance explains the definition and process for globally mobile employees.

Voluntarily payrolling other benefits

From 5 November 2026, employers can register to voluntarily payroll non-mandated benefits in kind (BiKs) for the 2027 to 2028 tax year using the online Payrolling Benefits and Expenses service.

Employers must register on or before 5 April 2027 to use this service. Employers already registered for voluntary payrolling will automatically be carried over to the 2027 to 2028 tax year.

Employers who voluntarily payroll non-mandated benefits must also account for associated Class 1A National Insurance contributions through payroll. They will no longer be able to report them separately at the end of the year.

Further changes from April 2028

Mandatory payrolling for most other benefits will be introduced from April 2028. Introducing the changes in phases will give employers more time to prepare and adapt in a manageable way.

HMRC thanks all agents who have been involved in any stakeholder engagement, by collaborating with us ahead of the latest guidance update.

Encourage your clients to prepare now if they have not already started. The updated guidance includes the latest details and examples, as well as a letter template to help employers explain the changes to employees.

Borders and trade

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — publication of CBAM rates

The UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will be introduced from 1 January 2027. CBAM will place a carbon price on highly traded, carbon intensive goods imported into the UK, so they face a comparable carbon price to the price that would be paid were the goods produced in the UK.

Sectors affected

From 1 January 2027 CBAM will apply to specific goods imported into the UK from the following sectors:

aluminium

cement

fertiliser

hydrogen

iron and steel

CBAM rates and default values

CBAM rates and default values were published on 16 October 2026 to help businesses prepare for the introduction of CBAM on 1 January 2027.

Agents should consider which clients may be affected by CBAM and encourage them to start preparing now.

To prepare for CBAM, businesses need to:

check whether their imports meet the £50,000 registration threshold and whether they will need to register when the service opens in January 2028

engage with their supply chain early to understand what emissions and carbon pricing information it can provide

use the published default values for reporting emissions if their supply chain cannot provide verified data

put processes in place to collect and keep the records they may need for CBAM reporting

More information

Read more on CBAM.

Learn more about the support available to tax agents and advisers which will help you and your clients.

The support for agents includes the publication of a series of webinars on CBAM this includes monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions, as well as Carbon Price Relief.

Changes for European Union indirect exports moving through Northern Ireland from 13 February 2027

HMRC is developing the Automated Export System (AES) to enable indirect export movements involving Northern Ireland.

AES will be introduced in 2 phases, with Phase 1 implemented on 13 February 2027. This is to fully digitalise the process for EU indirect exports — exports that start in an EU country and leave through Northern Ireland to a non-EU destination (including Great Britain).

To continue making EU indirect exports, from 13 February 2027, Economic Operators will be required to provide additional information about these goods movements after submitting the export declaration but before the goods arrive at an exit location in Northern Ireland.

When the AES Phase 1 goes live on 13 February 2027, HMRC will launch a free-to-use service and guidance enabling Economic Operators to submit this information.

The information can be completed by any Economic Operator involved in the movement, including agents. They can do so provided they have a UK issued Economic Operators Registration and Identification (EORI) or an EORI issued by an EU country (EU EORI), and are subscribed to the Customs Declaration Service (CDS).

If you’re an agent supporting traders making EU indirect exports and you’re not already subscribed to CDS, you must subscribe now, so you can access the new service from 13 February 2027.

Economic Operators with an EU EORI number will still need to subscribe to CDS to access the new service.

For indirect exports starting in Ireland and exiting through Northern Ireland, the new service will replace the alternative indirect export process, introduced in December 2025.

Further details about AES Phase 1 will be shared as we approach the 13 February 2027 deadline.

Phase 2 of AES will apply to goods movements starting in NI and exiting through an EU country to either GB or the rest of the world. There are no changes to the current processes for these movements and HMRC will share further details of AES Phase 2 closer to its launch.

Making Tax Digital

Making Tax Digital for Income Tax: check your clients’ 2025 to 2026 Self Assessment payment information

Since 9 November 2026, HMRC has begun writing to customers who were required to use Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. A copy of the letter can be found in the ‘customer communications’ section of the Agent Toolkit.

If you act for clients who are required to use MTD for Income Tax from 6 April 2026, their Self Assessment payment information may be shown across 2 accounts.

For payments due by 31 January 2027, this may include:

any balancing payment for the 2025 to 2026 tax year

the first payment on account for the 2026 to 2027 tax year

What you need to do

If you act for a client who has moved to MTD for Income Tax:

Check their existing Self Assessment statement for amounts due.

If an amount is marked ‘transferred to digital’, check their MTD for Income Tax account under ‘what you owe’.

Check both Self Assessment and MTD for Income Tax accounts to make sure you have identified all amounts your client needs to pay.

Make sure your client pays the amounts due by 31 January 2027. Moving to MTD for Income Tax does not change how much they owe or when they need to pay.

HMRC agent services

HMRC bulletin for Corporation Tax agents and advisers

Remind clients to submit their Company Tax returns

Every year, more than 100,000 companies fail to file their Company Tax return within 12 months of its statutory filing date. In May 2026, more than 20,000 companies had returns that were over a year late.

Companies must submit their Company Tax return by their statutory filing deadline, even if they have no Corporation Tax to pay.

HMRC may charge penalties for late returns. If a company does not file a return, HMRC may use the information it holds to issue a determination. This is an estimate of the Corporation Tax the company owes.

The company must still submit its return and pay any tax, interest, and penalties due.

Tax agents and advisers play an important role in helping companies meet their Corporation Tax obligations. However, the company and its directors remain legally responsible for meeting these obligations, even when an agent acts on their behalf.

If your clients have outstanding returns to file

Remind your clients to file any outstanding returns. This will help them to avoid being charged further late filing penalties, determinations, and compliance checks.

If a company has stopped trading, its directors should inform HMRC as soon as possible and file any outstanding returns. They may also wish to apply to have the company dissolved through Companies House, where appropriate.

Read more information on:

Corporation Tax

Accounting periods for Corporation Tax

Paying Corporation Tax

Filing a Company Tax Return

online applications to strike off and dissolve a company

Strike off a company from the Companies House register (DS01)

‘Be Ready’ campaign

The government’s new ‘Be Ready’ campaign helps people to take simple, practical steps to prepare for everyday risks and emergencies such as floods, fires and power cuts.

The principle behind it is simple: being prepared means frontline services can focus on those who need the most help during an emergency.

The Cabinet Office developed the campaign with input from the public.

Trusted partners supporting the campaign include:

the British Red Cross

National Emergencies Trust

local councils

emergency services

local resilience forums

Other countries have been running similar campaigns for many years, so this brings us into line with many of our neighbours.

Read and share the details of this important campaign with friends and family.

Changes to the ‘Where’s my reply’ tool

Customers can use the ‘Where’s my reply’ tool to check when they can expect to receive a response from HMRC to a query or request they made.

Agents can also use the tool to check how long HMRC is likely to take to:

process an application made on behalf of a client

process a request to change their agent details

Based on your feedback, we are improving the tool so you will now receive a more accurate response.

We are introducing the changes in stages, and we have focused on the 5 highest volume work areas:

SA appeals and penalties

Marriage Allowance

P87 — employment expense repayments

R40 claims for a refund of Income Tax deducted from certain types of income, particularly from savings and investment

registering for Self Assessment

Your feedback showed that the tool did not always give an accurate response time. In many cases, you received a reply sooner than the date shown. The changes mean most users will get a more realistic, expected reply date based on the normal timeframe for their request.

HMRC has achieved its target of clearing 80% of correspondence within 15 working days so far this year. If your request is taking longer, the tool will continue to show the longest expected waiting time, which is what happens now.

Once we have reviewed the first phase, we will be working on enhancing the tool to include all work areas.

Agents to use the Agent Dedicated Line for employer-related queries

We are encouraging all tax agents with employer-related queries to contact the Agent Dedicated Line, rather than the Employer Helpline.

This change is part of an ongoing trial. By bringing employer-related queries into the Agent Dedicated Line we will help provide a more consistent service for agents. This will help to make sure queries are handled by advisers with specialist knowledge of agents’ needs and the issues they encounter.

The trial will also give us greater insight to inform future improvements for agents.

The Employer Helpline will remain available for queries from individuals.

Top tips for Self Assessment

Every year we see common mistakes and avoidable issues in Self Assessment that can delay processing or create extra work for agents and their clients. These practical tips highlight some of the most frequent problems and explain what you can do to get things right.

Registering and reactivating for Self Assessment

Submitting a tax return for a client who has not registered for Self Assessment, or reactivated their Self Assessment record after a period of not filing, can lead to delays in processing, incorrect tax calculations and incorrect repayments.

Here’s how to get it right:

check if your client needs to complete a tax return

register new clients using the online CWF1 form for self-employed clients or the SA1 form for others

reactivate an existing Self Assessment record if your client already has a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) and needs to start filing again — use the online CWF1 or SA1 form to do this

you can also reactivate an account by calling the Agent Dedicated Line and selecting option 2, and then option 1 for ‘SA reactivations’ when prompted (note: if you select the wrong option, you won’t be redirected)

do not register a client as new if they already have a UTR (unless made bankrupt)

send the tax return when the notice to file (SA316) has been issued

Claims to carry back a trading or capital loss

We sometimes see claims to carry back a trading or capital loss omitted or completed incorrectly. This can delay processing and may require further contact with HMRC or an amended return.

Here’s how to get it right:

enter the relief in the correct tax calculation box:

paper filing: enter the relief amount (as a decrease in tax due) in box 15 or 16 on the Tax Calculation Summary (SA110)

online filing: use the ‘decrease in tax due because of an adjustment to an earlier year’ box

include details in the additional information box on the year the loss is being carried back to and the relevant legislation

submit the claim on the original tax return

Capital Gains: entering tax already charged correctly

We sometimes see errors when completing the residential property and carried interest section of the Capital Gains pages (SA108). Entering the wrong figure can result in incorrect tax calculations and delays in processing the return.

Here’s how to get it right:

when completing box 10, ‘Tax on gains in box 9 already charged’, enter the amount of tax due, not the amount paid

check the figure matches the tax previously charged on the disposal

include the payment reference shown on any previous documents relating to the earlier Capital Gains Tax charge in the additional information section of the return

review the Capital Gains pages before submission to make sure any previous tax charges have been reflected correctly

Check student and postgraduate loan information

We see frequent errors in the student or postgraduate loan section of the Self Assessment tax return. Mistakes can lead to incorrect student loan repayments being charged, which may affect the outstanding loan balance and the interest charged on the loan.

Here’s how to get it right:

check whether your client is currently repaying a student or postgraduate loan and ensure this is declared correctly on their tax return

select the correct loan plan or plans

check PAYE income and any student loan deductions already made through PAYE

check other relevant income, including self-employed profits and property income

check payrolled benefits in kind that are subject to Class 1A National Insurance contributions

Read more information on how to inform HMRC about a student loan in your tax return.

Recording Winter Fuel Payments

Customers in Self Assessment, who received a Winter Fuel Payment, or Pension Age Winter Heating Payment in Scotland, may need to include this in their tax return.

Here’s how to get it right:

If your client’s total income was over £35,000 you should include the Winter Fuel Payment or the Pension Age Winter Heating Payment on their return for the year in which they received it. For example, if your client received a payment in winter 2025, you would need to include it on their 2025 to 2026 tax return.

If you complete your client’s tax return using HMRC’s online service, we may pre-populate the payment. It will show as a Winter Fuel Payment charge or Pension Age Winter Heating Payment charge. You need to check if the payment is showing and include it if is not.

Read the guidance on Winter Fuel Payment: what to do if your income is over 35,000.

Bankruptcy — using the correct Unique Taxpayer Reference

We sometimes see Self Assessment returns submitted using a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) that is no longer valid following bankruptcy. This can delay processing and create unnecessary follow-up work.

Here’s how to get it right:

do not use the pre bankruptcy UTR for tax returns after the bankruptcy year. This UTR will have expired at the end of that year and is no longer valid

register the customer again for Self Assessment if they continue trading after the bankruptcy year or need to complete a Self Assessment tax return at any point after that year

ensure returns are submitted using the new UTR issued following registration

This allows HMRC to keep the customer’s pre and post‑bankruptcy tax affairs separate and ensures future returns are processed correctly.

Check you have a submission reference before chasing a repayment

When you submit a Self Assessment online repayment request, you’ll receive an on‑screen acknowledgement and submission reference confirming HMRC has received it.

In some cases, a client’s Self Assessment statement may continue to show a credit while the repayment request is being processed.

Here’s how to get it right:

check you have a submission reference — this confirms HMRC has received your repayment request

avoid submitting repeat repayment requests — if the account shows a credit but you have a submission reference, a further request is not needed, and it will not speed things up

reassure your client — a credit on their Self Assessment statement does not mean the request has been missed or rejected

check the ‘Where’s my reply’ tool for when you can expect a response and only contact HMRC if that time has passed

Make sure you are registered as a tax adviser

If you are paid for managing someone else’s tax affairs, then you must register with HMRC and set up an agent services account.

If you already have an agent services account, you will not need to register again.

Here’s how to get it right:

check if you need to register as a tax adviser

if you need to register, set up an HMRC agent services account and keep a record of your application reference

if you already have an agent services account, find your agent registration number (ARN)

have your agent registration number (ARN) or application reference available when contacting HMRC

From 19 November 2026 we may not be able to discuss your client’s record with you if you do not provide your ARN or application reference. This applies if you contact us by phone, post, online or by email.

Multi-factor authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds an extra layer of security to your agent online accounts.

If you have not signed in to your HMRC online services for agents account since MFA was introduced, you should do this as soon as possible as you’ll need to set your access preferences.

An MFA option may already be set up on your account. For example, someone in your organisation may have enabled it when using an HMRC service like Making Tax Digital for VAT. If this is the case, your access codes will be sent to the contact details saved when the option was set up.

Here’s how to get it right:

sign into your HMRC online services for agents account

if no previous MFA settings exist, you’ll choose how you get access codes when signing in for the first time

if previous preferences exist, locate the method or device used (voice call, text message or authenticator app) to receive your access code — once signed in, you can then update these if you wish

Read more information in the The Tax Agent’s Handbook.

Changes to paper 64-8 agent authorisation forms

HMRC is introducing changes to the way paper ‘64-8 Authorising your agent’ forms are processed.

From 2 December 2026, 64-8 forms must:

include the date of the client signature

be received by HMRC within 6 months of that signature date

Forms that do not meet these requirements will be sent a rejection letter explaining the reason for the rejection.

We’re making this change to ensure that client consent remains valid alongside the requirements for some agents to use advanced electronic signatures. This change is the latest in a range of measures HMRC has introduced to improve transparency in the agent market and provide further support to customers.

Further information is available on authorising an agent to deal with your tax affairs.

Multi-factor authentication: sign in after activation

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is now active on all agent accounts, adding an extra layer of security to help protect your account and your clients’ information from unauthorised access.

If you have not signed in since MFA was activated on your account, we recommend doing so as soon as possible to help maintain the security of your account.

Signing in now will also allow you to check that your access code method and settings are working as expected, helping to avoid delays or disruption when you next need to access your account to complete work on behalf of your clients.

Guidance and support

Full guidance remains available in the Tax Agent’s Handbook.

If you missed it, our recorded webinar is also still available, covering practical guidance on MFA and what to expect: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars for tax agents and advisers.

Help shape the future of Corporation Tax

The government is continuing to work to modernise Corporation Tax, creating a simpler system that makes better use of technology and data, while working closely with stakeholders on the changes.

The government has published the Modernising and standardising Company Tax returns — summary of responses to the 2026 consultation. This sets out a longer, more flexible timetable for prescribed Corporation Tax computations to allow more time for review, refinement and testing before implementation. This work will improve Corporation Tax reporting in the immediate term and provide the integral data foundation for long term modernisation of Corporation Tax administration.

At Autumn Budget 2026, the government also announced 2 opportunities for stakeholders to help shape future changes.

Modernising Corporation Tax administration call for evidence

The call for evidence for the Modernising Corporation Tax administration is open until 20 January 2027. It seeks long-term strategic views on how Corporation Tax is administered in practice, including how it could better meet users’ needs, support compliance, reduce duplication and make better use of technology, data and digital services.

Queries and feedback on the call for evidence can be sent by email to ctmodernisation@hmrc.gov.uk.

Corporate Tax Simplification for Business Investment

The Corporate Tax Simplification for Business Investment work sets out a targeted programme to simplify areas of the Corporate Tax system where stakeholders have raised concerns about complexity, uncertainty and administrative burdens. It aims to improve certainty and support investment, growth and competitiveness.

Over the next year, the government will work with stakeholders to develop, prioritise and test options for meaningful reform. Those with relevant experience of the Corporation Tax system are invited to express an interest by 21 November 2026 by email to ct.simplification@hmrc.gov.uk.

While each of these strands has a slightly different focus and is at a different stage of development, they form part of the same direction of travel towards a modern Corporation Tax system. This work will help shape a simpler, more modern Corporation Tax system, informed by stakeholder experience.

HMRC is working closely across government on Modernising corporate reporting to ensure that changes to Corporation Tax administration and the wider corporate reporting framework are aligned.

Reminder: Time to Pay support is available

If a customer is unable to pay their tax bill in full and on time, a Time to Pay arrangement may be an option. It can allow customers to repay what they owe in affordable instalments based on their circumstances.

You can read more information about the support available if you cannot pay your tax bill on time.

Tax adviser registration: update for existing agent services account holders

If you already have an agent services account (ASA), you do not need to register again. We will contact you during the 2027 to 2028 financial year if we need more information to check if you meet certain conditions

We will publish further guidance before this process starts.

Agent engagement

Modernising HMRC’s approach to wealthy compliance

HMRC has published a new multi-year plan setting out how it will modernise its approach to wealthy customers. It aims to do this by using better data, technology and specialist expertise to make it easier to get tax right, improve customer experience and identify and address non-compliance earlier.

The changes are part of HMRC’s wider transformation, allowing it to better understand increasingly complex customer affairs, reduce unnecessary contact and focus specialist resource where the risks are greatest.

The plan has been developed with input from advisers, professional bodies and academics, whose expertise and insights have helped inform its content and direction. HMRC has worked closely with them and listened to their views on the key elements of the plan, supporting our commitment to ensure a more transparent approach and to hold us to account.

Read more information on HMRC’s approach to wealthy compliance plan.
